items: Schedule a vet appointment immediately if your cat strains to urinate with little output, cries in the litter box, has blood in urine, or shows lethargy alongside avoidance behavior.
Request a urinalysis test that checks for infection, crystals, and blood when you visit the vet for litter box avoidance issues.
Ask your vet to run a full blood panel that rules out kidney disease, diabetes, and hyperthyroidism as potential medical causes.
Do not accept a behavioral diagnosis without medical testing — insist on urinalysis, blood work, and bladder palpitation before treating the issue as environmental.
Add one litter box per cat plus one extra, placing them in separate areas of your home to eliminate territorial sharing disputes.
Switch from a covered litter box to an uncovered one because covered boxes trap ammonia odor inside, which overwhelms sensitive feline noses.
Replace scented litter with unscented clumping litter at minimum 2-inch depth, since strong fragrances are a common avoidance trigger for cats.
Scoop the litter box at least once daily and completely empty and clean it with hot water and mild soap every 4–6 weeks.
Look for signs of multi-cat tension including one cat waiting near the box, chasing behavior, increased hiding, or dispute-like vocalizations that may be driving avoidance.
Add vertical space with cat trees or shelves so the targeted cat can escape tension and access the box without confrontation.
Separate food and water stations for each cat in different locations to reduce competition that contributes to stress-related elimination problems.
Use Feliway Classic diffusers to reduce baseline stress in multi-cat homes since peer-reviewed studies demonstrate it decreases stress-related inappropriate urination.
